More about this
What do the triggers mean?
Bristol stool form scale

The Bristol scale sorts stool into seven types by its form. The form shows how quickly the gut contents moved along: the longer they stay in the large intestine, the more water is drawn out and the firmer they get.

Types 3 to 5 count as normal, type 4 as ideal. Types 1 and 2 point to slow transit (constipation), types 6 and 7 to fast transit (diarrhoea). The form also varies with food, fluid intake, exercise and stress, so the course over several days matters more than a single bowel movement.
After Lewis and Heaton (1997). The drawings were made for this app.
Rating symptoms

Rate each symptom from 0 to 10, by its worst moment since your last entry. Entries are most meaningful when you log them as soon as something happens. The app doesn\'t save a slider you haven\'t touched. Feel free to log a 0 when you want to record that something was not there.
What the scale means
0 – none: nothing to feel.
1–3 – mild: noticeable, but everyday life goes on as normal.
4–6 – moderate: clearly bothersome, you have to take it into account.
7–10 – severe: dominates everything, you need a break or have to lie down.
Under Analysis → Connections, a symptom counts from severity 4. You can change this in the analysis settings.
The belly feels tight, bloated or too full, even if nothing shows from the outside.
Pain or cramps anywhere in the belly. If they come right before a bowel movement, also note that with the bowel movement.
Passing wind more often or more unpleasantly than usual.
From a queasy stomach to the urge to vomit.
Unusual exhaustion, for example after eating.
Headaches of any kind. Some people get them after alcohol or food high in histamine, for example.
Triggers

Triggers are properties of foods that cause symptoms in some people. Each ingredient carries the triggers that apply to it; a dish has the triggers of its ingredients. Some only apply from a certain amount, such as “from L”.

Lactose, fructose, polyols, fructans and GOS belong to the FODMAPs: short-chain carbohydrates that are poorly absorbed in the small intestine and fermented by bacteria in the large intestine. This produces gas and draws water into the gut. In irritable bowel syndrome they often cause bloating, pain and diarrhoea.

The most reliable way to find out whether a trigger really leads to symptoms is an elimination diet followed by step-by-step reintroduction, guided by a dietitian or doctor. Don\'t cut out many foods for good on your own.
Milk sugar. If the enzyme lactase is missing in the small intestine, it reaches the large intestine and is fermented there.
Milk, yoghurt, quark, cream, cream cheese, ice cream. Long-matured hard cheese contains hardly any lactose.
Hydrogen breath test with lactose, possibly a genetic test.
Fruit sugar. It is poorly absorbed when a food contains more fructose than glucose (fructose malabsorption).
Apples, pears, mango, honey, agave syrup, fruit juices.
Hydrogen breath test with fructose. The rare inborn (hereditary) fructose intolerance must be ruled out first.
Sugar alcohols such as sorbitol, mannitol and xylitol. They are only partly absorbed and draw water into the gut.
Plums, apricots, cherries, pears, mushrooms, cauliflower, sugar-free chewing gum and sweets.
No standard test; usually a guided elimination diet.
Chains of fruit sugar that humans cannot digest. One of the most common triggers in irritable bowel syndrome.
Wheat, rye, onion, garlic, leek.
No lab test; a guided low-FODMAP elimination diet with reintroduction.
Galacto-oligosaccharides, sugars from pulses that are fermented in the large intestine.
Beans, lentils, chickpeas, soybeans.
No lab test; a guided low-FODMAP elimination diet with reintroduction.

A protein in wheat, rye, barley and spelt. Important in coeliac disease (an autoimmune disease) and wheat allergy. In irritable bowel syndrome, symptoms after wheat are often due to fructans rather than gluten.
Bread, rolls, pasta, cakes and pastries, breadcrumb coating, beer.
Blood test for coeliac antibodies (tissue transglutaminase IgA with total IgA), possibly a small-bowel biopsy. Important: don\'t eat gluten-free before the test, or it may come back falsely negative.
A messenger substance that forms in matured and fermented foods. Histamine intolerance is scientifically disputed and hard to prove.
Matured cheese, salami, cured ham, sauerkraut, red wine, canned tuna, tomatoes, spinach.
No reliable lab test; measuring the enzyme DAO in the blood says little. A guided elimination diet with targeted reintroduction.
Fatty food stays in the stomach longer and stimulates the gut more strongly.
Fried food, schnitzel, chips, cream, sausages, cakes and pastries.
No test of its own. With greasy, foul-smelling stool, have the pancreas (faecal elastase) and gallbladder checked.
Stimulates bowel movements and can thus encourage diarrhoea.
Coffee, black and green tea, cola, energy drinks.
Leaving it out for a while.
Irritates the gut lining and speeds up transit.
Beer, wine, sparkling wine, spirits.
Leaving it out for a while.
Capsaicin from chilli irritates pain receptors in the gut and can trigger cramps and diarrhoea.
Chilli, hot peppers, hot paprika, curries.
Leaving it out for a while.
The gas stretches the stomach and gut and can cause bloating and burping.
Sparkling water, soft drinks, beer, sparkling wine.
Leaving it out for a while.
Irritable bowel syndrome

Doctors describe irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) using the Rome IV criteria: recurring abdominal pain, on average at least one day a week over the last three months, with at least two of these features:
The pain is related to bowel movements.
It comes with a change in how often you pass stool.
It comes with a change in stool form.
The symptoms started at least six months before the diagnosis.

For the conversation with your doctor, precise records help: whether you had abdominal pain or cramps before a bowel movement and whether they were better, the same or worse afterwards, what form the stool had (Bristol type) and how often you go. The app does not check these criteria and does not say whether you have IBS.
A doctor makes the diagnosis after ruling out other causes such as coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease. Your records help with the conversation.
Please see a doctor soon

Blood in the stool or black stool · unintended weight loss · fever · symptoms that wake you at night · new symptoms from around age 50 · anaemia · bowel cancer, coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease in the family.
Purpose, privacy, sources & licence
What LogMyGut is for

LogMyGut is a diary for food, drinks, bowel movements and symptoms. It shows your own entries as overviews and counts how often symptoms were logged after meals with certain triggers. LogMyGut is not a medical device: it does not diagnose, does not detect diseases or intolerances, and does not give treatment or diet recommendations. You can take the overviews to your doctor or dietitian. Don\'t change your diet or medication based on this app alone. With severe or new symptoms, get medical help.
Your data
All entries stay on this device. The app has no internet access, sends nothing and makes no cloud backup. So you are responsible for backups yourself: Settings → Backup.
